questions.question: If n = p·q with p, q distinct primes, what is φ(n)?
options: n − 1, the count of non-zero residues in Z/nZ
(p − 1)·(q − 1), the count of integers in [1,n] coprime to n
p + q − 1, since each prime contributes its index to n
(p − 1) + (q − 1), summing residues coprime to each factor
questions.explanation: φ is multiplicative on coprime factors. φ(p) = p−1, φ(q) = q−1, so φ(pq) = (p−1)(q−1).

questions.question: Why must RSA know `φ(n)` and yet keep it secret?
options: Needed to pick e; knowing φ(n) lets anyone factor n trivially via Euler
Needed to compute d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n); knowing it lets anyone recover d
Needed only during encryption; safe to publish alongside the modulus n
Not needed at all; RSA uses Carmichael λ(n) instead in modern variants
questions.explanation: d ≡ e⁻¹ (mod φ(n)). Anyone with φ(n) computes d. Equivalent to factoring n since φ(n) and n determine p, q via a quadratic.

questions.question: Euler's totient `φ(n)` for general n = p₁^a₁ · … · pₖ^aₖ equals:
options: n · ∏(1 − 1/pᵢ) over distinct prime factors pᵢ of n
n − ∑pᵢ subtracting each prime once from the modulus
∏(pᵢ − 1) ignoring the exponent of each prime in n
n / ∏pᵢ dividing out one copy of each distinct prime
questions.explanation: φ(n) = n · ∏(1 − 1/p) over distinct primes p | n. Equivalent: ∏ pᵢ^(aᵢ−1)·(pᵢ − 1).

questions.question: What does Carmichael's λ(n) compute, and how does it relate to φ(n)?
options: λ(n) is φ(n) divided by the number of distinct prime factors of n
λ(n) is the exponent of (Z/nZ)*: smallest k with a^k ≡ 1 for all coprime a; λ(n) | φ(n)
λ(n) is the order of the largest cyclic subgroup of (Z/nZ)*; equal to φ(n) only when n is prime
λ(n) is the count of primitive roots mod n, always strictly less than φ(n)
questions.explanation: λ(n) = exponent of the unit group: smallest k with a^k ≡ 1 (mod n) ∀ gcd(a,n)=1. Always λ(n) | φ(n); often strictly smaller.

questions.question: For RSA n = p·q with distinct primes, what is λ(n)?
options: λ(n) = (p − 1)·(q − 1) = φ(n) — they always coincide for two-prime RSA
λ(n) = lcm(p − 1, q − 1) — can be much smaller than φ(n) for some primes
λ(n) = gcd(p − 1, q − 1) — always small, hence avoided in RSA design
λ(n) = p + q − 1 — derives from the sum of orders of subgroups
questions.explanation: λ(pq) = lcm(p−1, q−1). PKCS#1 v2 uses d = e⁻¹ mod λ(n) for a shorter private exponent (still secure).

questions.question: Compute φ(36).
options: 10, counting residues less than half of 36 that are prime
18, half of 36 since 2 divides 36 evenly with no further reduction
20, counting odd residues less than 36 that avoid the factor 3

questions.question: If an attacker learns φ(n) for an RSA modulus n = p·q, how do they factor n?
options: Solve the quadratic x² − (n − φ(n) + 1)·x + n = 0; roots are p, q
Compute gcd(φ(n), n); the result equals p, the smaller prime factor
Apply Fermat factorization starting from ⌈√φ(n)⌉ instead of ⌈√n⌉
Run Miller-Rabin with φ(n) as the witness base to identify p, q quickly
questions.explanation: p + q = n − φ(n) + 1 and p·q = n. Roots of x² − (p+q)x + pq = 0 are p, q. Hence knowing φ(n) ⇔ knowing the factorization.

questions.question: Why must RSA primes p, q never be chosen so that p − 1 and q − 1 share a large smooth common factor?
options: Then λ(n) = lcm(p−1, q−1) is small, making d small and exposing it to brute force
Then φ(n) becomes divisible by 4, breaking the Euler-based decryption identity
Then gcd(p, q) > 1, violating RSA's distinct-prime requirement at key generation
Then Carmichael numbers appear in (Z/nZ)*, defeating Miller-Rabin verification
questions.explanation: Small λ(n) makes the order of every element small. Pollard p−1 also exploits smooth p−1. Use safe primes (p = 2p′+1 with p′ prime).
